items.key: ai:men in their 20s are already seeking help for hair loss: here's what the data shows
items.text: Men In Their 20s Are Already Seeking Help For Hair Loss: Here's What The Data Shows
items.article: Among men under 25, receding hairlines were a more common concern; after 35, thinning and low volume took the lead. Hair loss may still be associated with getting older, but two large datasets of Indian men seeking help for hair loss suggest that the concern is appearing much earlier than many might assume. An analysis of more than 12.6 lakh hair-loss consultations and assessments from Man Matters and Traya Health shows a consistent pattern: men are seeking help for hair loss predominantly in their 20s and early 30s, while a significant number are already experiencing noticeable progression when they do. The datasets are separate and cover different consultation populations and periods. The Man Matters Hairfall Index 2026 analysed 704,152 consultations conducted between August 2025 and August 2026, while a Traya Health study looked at 561,960 Indian men seeking help for hair loss. Together, the numbers offer a snapshot of when men start seeking help, what they notice first and how hair loss appears to progress with age. The Man Matters data found that 87.2% of hairfall consultations came from men under 35, with men in their 20s accounting for a significant share of the consultation base. Traya’s study similarly found that the median age of men experiencing hair loss was 29, with 76.4% of those assessed below 35. items.text: I was in my 30s when I started suffering unexplained stomach problems, fatigue and mood swings. To my shock, it turned out to be perimenopause. This is why it can start earlier than you think
items.article: Perimenopause can begin in your 30s. Discover the lesser-known symptoms, from digestive issues and migraines to fatigue and mood swings. Your stomach cramps, your head pounds and there’s a foggy feeling in your brain that just won’t shift. For many women in their 30s, symptoms such as brain fog, chronic fatigue, digestive issues and migraines are commonplace. When they book a consultation with their doctor, they are dismissed with diagnoses of stress, Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) or lifestyle fatigue. But what if these symptoms, when put together, could reveal another cause? The reality behind these unexpected problems could actually be something rarely discussed in younger age groups: perimenopause. While the conversation around midlife hormonal shifts has grown in recent years, misconceptions about when this transition begins, and how long it might last, are still rife. Around one in 100 women experience menopause before the age of 40, a condition medically defined as Primary Ovarian Insufficiency (POI). Yet millions more in their late 30s begin experiencing the early, turbulent waves of perimenopause without realising it. Sonia Dunleavy, 50, from Buckinghamshire, was just 42 when she went through menopause.
